summary: Moldova is a landlocked country in Eastern Europe between Romania and Ukraine, known for its wine industry; the area along the Dniester River in the east has been controlled by separatist forces since the 1990s.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: The Principality of Moldavia made Orthodoxy its state religion from the 14th century, and rulers such as Prince Stephen the Great built many monasteries. Religion was suppressed during the Soviet period, but after independence in 1991 the church revived rapidly, and Orthodoxy became the faith of the great majority of Moldovans and part of their cultural identity. The church is divided into the pro-Russian Orthodox Church of Moldova and the pro-Romanian Metropolis of Bessarabia, and after the Russo-Ukrainian war in 2022 the number of clergy switching to the latter increased.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: These include Catholics (mainly of Polish descent and some Ukrainians), Baptists and Pentecostals (introduced in the late Soviet period and after independence), Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses. These denominations have grown under the religious freedom since independence.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: During half a century of Soviet rule atheist education was promoted, but after independence Orthodoxy revived rapidly, and very few people explicitly call themselves non-religious, mainly some residents of cities.

religion.background: Bessarabia, where Moldova is located, belonged to the Principality of Moldavia in the Middle Ages; from the 14th century Orthodoxy became the state religion, and under Byzantine and Bulgarian influence Church Slavonic liturgy was used. In the 15th century Prince Stephen the Great built many monasteries and resisted the Ottoman Empire. In 1812 the Russian Empire annexed Bessarabia and the church was incorporated into the Russian Orthodox Church system. From 1918 to 1940 Bessarabia belonged to Romania, and after 1940 it became part of the Soviet Union, which promoted atheism and closed large numbers of churches and monasteries. After independence in 1991 Orthodoxy revived rapidly, but the church split into the Orthodox Church of Moldova under the Moscow Patriarchate and the Metropolis of Bessarabia under the Romanian church, reflecting divisions in national identity.

ranking.name: Romanian
ranking.description: Romanian derives from the Latin of the Roman period and is the mother tongue of the great majority in Moldova. In the Soviet period it was called "Moldovan" and written in the Cyrillic alphabet to downplay ties with Romania; the Latin alphabet was restored in 1989, and in 2023 parliament formally confirmed the name of the official language as Romanian.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: After the Russian Empire annexed Bessarabia in 1812, Russian became the language of administration, and in the Soviet period it was promoted even more strongly and large numbers of Russian and Ukrainian immigrants were brought in. Today Russian is still widely used, especially in the capital Chișinău and the separatist Transnistria region (which declared independence in 1990 and is not under central control).

ranking.name: Gagauz
ranking.description: The Gagauz are an Orthodox Christian Turkic people who migrated in the 18th–19th centuries from the Balkans (present-day northeastern Bulgaria) to southern Bessarabia. Their language, Gagauz, is close to Turkish; in 1994 Moldova established the Gagauz Autonomous Region, and Gagauz became one of the official languages locally.

ranking.name: Ukrainian
ranking.description: Ukrainian speakers are mainly found in the north and along the Dniester, areas bordering Ukraine where Ukrainian peasants have lived since the Middle Ages. In the Soviet period many Ukrainians switched to speaking Russian, so the population that actually uses Ukrainian is smaller than the ethnic Ukrainian population.

language.history: The Moldovan language and Romanian are in fact the same language, derived from the Latin left by the Roman Empire in the region of Dacia. In the Middle Ages the Principality of Moldavia wrote Romanian in the Cyrillic alphabet; in the 19th century Romania switched to the Latin alphabet, but Bessarabia, annexed by Russia in 1812, continued to use Cyrillic. In the Soviet period, to set it apart from Romania, "Moldovan" was declared a separate language, written in Cyrillic, and Russian was promoted. In 1989 Moldova restored the Latin alphabet and in 1991 became independent; in 2013 the Constitutional Court ruled that the official language is Romanian, and in 2023 parliament formally amended the law to change "Moldovan" to "Romanian" in all legislation.

ranking.name: Mămăligă (cornmeal mush)
ranking.description: A thick yellow porridge cooked from cornmeal and water, often eaten with cheese, sour cream, scrambled eggs or stewed meat. It has a creamy, dense texture and a mild flavor, and is mainly used to accompany other dishes.
ranking.history: Corn was introduced to Moldavia from the Americas via the Ottoman Empire in the 17th century, and because of its high yield and suitability to the local climate it gradually replaced millet as the farmers' staple. In the past poor farm families used mămăligă in place of bread, and both Moldova and Romania regard it as a national dish. Today it is a common staple at festivals and family meals, often served together with sarmale.

ranking.name: Plăcintă
ranking.description: A round or square pie of thin dough filled with cheese, potato, cabbage, pumpkin or fruit, which can be baked or fried. It has a crisp crust and varied fillings and can be eaten as breakfast, a snack or with soup.
ranking.history: The name plăcintă comes from the Latin placenta (flat cake), reflecting the linguistic and culinary influence left in Dacia from Roman times. It is Moldova's most common home-style snack, and almost every family has its own recipe. At festivals, weddings and memorial rites, plăcintă is often distributed to relatives, friends and neighbors.

ranking.name: Sarmale (cabbage rolls)
ranking.description: Rolls of pickled cabbage leaves or grape leaves wrapped around minced meat and rice and slowly stewed in tomato sauce. They taste tangy, with tender meat filling, and are often eaten with sour cream.
ranking.history: The name sarmale comes from the Turkish sarma (rolled up), reflecting the culinary influence the Principality of Moldavia received during the 16th–19th centuries as a vassal of the Ottoman Empire. In Moldova, sarmale is an essential dish at festivals such as Christmas, New Year and weddings, eaten together with mămăligă and symbolizing abundance and reunion.

ranking.name: Zeamă (chicken soup)
ranking.description: A clear broth simmered from home-raised chicken, with homemade noodles, vegetables and sour fermented wheat-bran liquid (borș) added, sprinkled with fresh herbs.
ranking.history: Zeamă is Moldova's most representative soup; its sourness comes from borș, made by fermenting wheat bran, a seasoning method unique to Moldova and Romania. Traditionally it uses free-range chickens raised at home and is made on weekends and at festivals; it is also regarded as a remedy for hangovers and colds, and is the dish that most evokes home for Moldovans.

ranking.name: Mititei
ranking.description: Small skinless sausages made of ground beef, pork or lamb with garlic and spices, grilled over charcoal and eaten with mustard and bread. They are charred outside and juicy inside, with a strong garlic aroma.
ranking.history: Mititei means "little ones" and is generally thought to have originated in a restaurant in Bucharest, Romania, in the 19th century; legend says a cook, having run out of sausage casings, grilled the meat mixture directly. It was influenced by Ottoman and Balkan grilled meats (such as ćevapi), and today it is an essential food for summer barbecues and for picnics on 1 May Labor Day in Moldova and Romania.
